intro: Ernest White recorded Messiaen’s La Nativité du Seigneur in August 1949 on the rebuilt Walcker organ of Memorial Hall, Methuen, Massachusetts. This is the ninth and last piece, Dieu parmi nous, which ends in a toccata.

sections.label: A · Loud opening, then quieter music

cues.title: Ninth and last meditation
cues.text: Dieu parmi nous closes the nine meditations. Messiaen printed three scriptural passages above it, including “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us”, and paired it with the seventh piece as the living, sorrowing God in our midst.
cues.evidence: Preface to the score (flyleaf) and the epigraph to piece 9 (Ecclesiasticus 24; John 1:14; Luke 1:46–47), as printed in English on the Mercury Classics MG 10069 sleeve (notes on the composer, the music, the artist and the organ), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur-the-nativ_ernest-white-olivier-messiaen.

cues.title: The Methuen organ
cues.text: The organ was built by Walcker in 1857–62. It stood in the Boston Music Hall from 1863 to 1884 and was heard in Methuen’s Memorial Hall from 1909. G. Donald Harrison of Aeolian-Skinner redesigned it, and the recording used the rebuilt instrument.
cues.evidence: History of the organ in the sleeve note “The artist and his instrument”: the Mercury Classics MG 10069 sleeve (notes on the composer, the music, the artist and the organ), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur-the-nativ_ernest-white-olivier-messiaen . Walcker 1863, rebuilt by Aeolian-Skinner 1949: The American Organist, October 1952 (vol. 35, no. 10), record reviews: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-organist-1918_1952-10_35_10

cues.title: Loud section begins
cues.text: The organ becomes much louder here and stays loud, apart from short dips, to the end of the piece.
cues.evidence: Heard in the transfer of Mercury MG 10069, side 2: after a near-silent moment at about 2:25 the sound jumps to its loud passages, the largest rise in the track, and stays there with brief dips to the end.

cues.title: Ernest White
cues.text: Ernest White was born in Canada and went to the United States in 1925 to study the organ with Lynnwood Farnam. He became musical director of the Church of St Mary the Virgin in New York.
cues.evidence: Sleeve note “The artist and his instrument”: the Mercury Classics MG 10069 sleeve (notes on the composer, the music, the artist and the organ), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur-the-nativ_ernest-white-olivier-messiaen

cues.title: Recording and issue, 1949–52
cues.text: The sleeve says the recording was made in August 1949 under the engineering supervision of H. Vose Greenough. Mercury issued it as MG 10069 at $4.85, and The American Organist reviewed it in October 1952.
cues.evidence: Session and engineer: the Mercury Classics MG 10069 sleeve (notes on the composer, the music, the artist and the organ), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur-the-nativ_ernest-white-olivier-messiaen . Issue and price: The American Organist, October 1952 (vol. 35, no. 10), record reviews: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-organist-1918_1952-10_35_10

cues.title: Messiaen at twenty-six
cues.text: Messiaen wrote La Nativité in 1935, in Grenoble, at the age of twenty-six. His preface to the score begins: “Emotion and sincerity above all!”
cues.evidence: Preface as quoted on the Mercury Classics MG 10069 sleeve (notes on the composer, the music, the artist and the organ), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur-the-nativ_ernest-white-olivier-messiaen . Composition in Grenoble, summer 1935: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Nativit%C3%A9_du_Seigneur

cues.title: First performance, 1936
cues.text: Three organists shared the first performance at La Trinité on 27 February 1936: Daniel-Lesur played pieces 1–3, Jean Langlais 4–6 and Jean-Jacques Grunenwald 7–9, which include this one. Leduc published piece 9 alone as the fourth book.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Nativit%C3%A9_du_Seigneur (première on 27 February 1936; division among the players; Book IV for piece 9 alone).

cues.title: Two reviews, 1952
cues.text: The American Organist called the cycle “difficult-to-play and difficult-to-enjoy” but said White’s performance should satisfy admirers of the work. Mildred Andrews of the University of Oklahoma, quoted in American Music Teacher, called him “a musical architect of real genius”.
cues.evidence: The American Organist, October 1952 (vol. 35, no. 10), record reviews: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-organist-1918_1952-10_35_10 . American Music Teacher, November–December 1952 (vol. 2, no. 2), record reviews: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-music-teacher_november-december-1952_2_2

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: “Ernest White playing the Memorial Hall Organ, Methuen, Mass.” on the sleeve; The American Organist of October 1952 lists the disc under “Ernest White, Methuen Memorial Hall, Mass.”. The sleeve names H. Vose Greenough as supervising engineer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Organ cycle of 1935, published by Leduc in 1936; movement IX of nine, ending in a toccata.
fields.note: The sleeve calls the work “The Nativity of Our Lord (published in 1936)”; Wikipedia gives Leduc as publisher and says movement IX alone formed the fourth book; Gillian Weir’s programme note describes the piece as ending in a toccata. The sleeve does not name an edition.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The sleeve says “the present recording was accomplished in August of 1949”. The day is not given. The Internet Archive’s date of 1952 for the item is the year of issue, not of the session.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The sleeve names the “newly rebuilt organ at Memorial Hall in Methuen, Mass.”, an instrument originally built by Walcker in 1857–62 for the Boston Music Hall and redesigned under G. Donald Harrison of Aeolian-Skinner.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The Internet Archive record gives publisher Mercury Classics. The sleeve names the Mercury Classics label and, in its note on the artist, three earlier Ernest White discs on the same label (MG 10070, MG 15032, MG 15027).

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The sleeve prints “MG 10069”; The American Organist (October 1952) lists it at $4.85 and American Music Teacher (November–December 1952) reviews it. The Internet Archive record dates the item 1952.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 2, track 5 of the Internet Archive segmentation (“God Among Us”); matrix and take numbers not read
fields.note: The track list on the sleeve gives nine pieces in order. The transferred track is the last on side 2, 428.5 seconds long.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation; the ripping operator is not credited by name
fields.note: The item sits in the Internet Archive’s Boston Public Library and other vinyl collections. Collection membership does not establish the original session.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: From the ripping_date field (20191008). The sleeve was scanned on 18 September 2019.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable, Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge, Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp and Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; side recorded to FLAC and segmented into a VBR MP3 per track.
fields.note: The lineage field states the signal chain. The final segmentation of this track is 890.892–1319.348 seconds of the side-2 capture, differing from an automatic start at 915.943 seconds, which suggests a manual correction. The level trace suggests that the first 1.3 seconds carry the end of the previous piece, followed by a short pause before the music of this piece begins at about 1.9 seconds; this is inferred from the trace, not heard. Equalisation, de-clicking and speed correction are not described. The pitch measured from the audio is about 32 cents (roughly a third of a semitone) above A = 440 Hz and steady; the organ’s tuning cannot be separated from the speed of the original recording or the transfer.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Messiaen died in 1992, so the work is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2062.
fields.note: The death year is taken from the Wikipedia article’s dates for Messiaen (1908–1992); the term is our calculation. Rights in the composition are separate from rights in the recording. No United States status is claimed.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: first published by autumn 1952 (before 1963); US status not established.
fields.note: Two American periodicals of autumn 1952 review the disc, so it had been published by then. The first-issue date is not established and may be earlier; the session was in 1949. An EU phonogram published in 1952 had run its 50-year term by the end of 2002 and was not revived by the 2011 extension, which applies to fixations still protected on 1 November 2013. No United States clearance is claimed. The Internet Archive item carries no licence.

Vose Greenough); Mercury Classics MG 10069, reviewed in The American Organist, October 1952. Internet Archive vinyl transfer, October 2019. Territorial EU public-domain recording basis; US status not established.

composer.background:
Olivier Messiaen was born in Avignon at midnight on 10 December 1908, and his grandfather marked the birth by singing the old carol Il est né, le divin enfant. His mother, Cécile Sauvage, had written L’Âme en bourgeon while she was expecting him. He later said there had been “only one influence in my life, and it happened before I was born”. At seven and a half, in wartime Grenoble, he sat on a bench in the town park reading the vocal score of Gluck’s Orphée and realised he could hear it in his head. “So, I was a musician,” he recalled. He also staged Shakespeare for his brother Alain, using cardboard figures and coloured cellophane from sweet boxes, with sunlight to light the theatre. Their father, an English teacher and Shakespeare translator, was away at the front. Olivier taught himself the piano. At ten, in Nantes, his teacher Jean de Gibon gave him Debussy’s Pelléas et Mélisande, and he played and sang it until he knew it by heart. Writing about himself in 1970, he said that the mountains of the Dauphiné “are his true home”.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1919, studying composition with Paul Dukas, music history with Maurice Emmanuel, and organ with Marcel Dupré. In 1931, aged twenty-two, he became organist of La Trinité. He kept the job for the rest of his life. The church divided his Sundays between plainchant, older concert music and his own compositions. At vespers he improvised, because the short intervals in the service left no room for complete pieces.
